2.text: “There was a small girl Yɪˊnkɪ-ñeˊut by name. Some people had gathered in a tent to per-

3.text: form a thanksgiving ceremonial. They darkened the vent-hole, and began to sing. Still they were

4.text: not men, but dogs. Some sang, ‘Koo, koo, koo!’ Others howled, ‘Koon, koon, koon!’¹ Then

5.text: the house mistress said to the girl, ‘Look there! Who are those singers? Why have they closed the

6.text: entrance and darkened the vent-hole?’ The girl found a crevice, and peeped through it. They

7.text: were all dogs. The Chukchee people came hastily and gave them blows. The dogs fled to the

8.text: west and became Russian people. Some of them, however, remained dogs, and were used by the

9.text: others for driving. Those that were beaten got angry at the blows and began a war. O dear!

10.text: we did not know. Our people chastized the dogs, and they became a people.”²

11.text: A story like this, of course, could be found only among the reindeer-

12.text: breeders, in opposition to the Russian dog-drivers.

13.text: Almost all tales mention the name of Yäkuˊnnin, the chief of the Cossacks.

14.text: This name is given to Major Pavlutsky.³ Its origin could not be ascertained.

15.text: It is allied to the Russian name Яковъ, pronounced Yakov (“James”); but the

16.text: first name of Pavlutsky was Theodore, not James. Yäkuˊnnin is described as

17.text: strong and tall, clad in glistening iron, shining white like a large white gull

18.text: (Larus argentatus). He stands before a crowd of Chukchee in full armor,

19.text: springs up as high as the highest tree, and brandishes his spear. He has a

20.text: step-son, or an adopted son, from the reindeer-breeding people, either Koryak

21.text: or Chukchee, — a good warrior, who aids Yäkuˊnnin in many ways. The

22.text: defeat of Yäkuˊnnin is preceded by the misadventure of his assistant. In some

23.text: versions the adopted son of Yäkuˊnnin, who is called Young Yäkuˊnnin, is

24.text: taken prisoner and killed. In other versions, when taken a prisoner, he con-

25.text: sents to commit treason, and brings Chukchee scouts to the Russian camp.

26.text: In still other stories he gives information which makes it possible for the Chuk-

27.text: chee to lay hold of the provisions of the Russians. Some of the details

28.text: correspond in a certain degree to the real facts. Pavlutsky and his Cossacks,

29.text: as well as many other Cossack expeditions, had an auxiliary detachment of

30.text: Tungus, Chuvantzy, and even Koryak, driving reindeer and conveying food.

31.text: They took part in the campaign half against their wills, and afterwards broke

32.text: out in open mutiny, or simply left the Cossacks at an opportune moment.

33.text: In the detachment of Pavlutsky there was even some quarreling among the

34.text: Cossacks of local birth and the infantry that he brought along from Yakutsk.

43.text: ³ Argentoff mentions the name Pavluchka as used in Chukchee traditions. I could not find this mentioned,

44.text: in the papers of Argentoff, but have met with it in an article in a Russian review, that related to one of my

45.text: own papers. The article mentions that the paper by Argentoff in question here is very rare, and has appeared

46.text: in Siberia. I have not come across the name Pavluchka in Chukchee stories and traditions. The Chukchee,
